title: Postoperatively Adjustable Breast Implant -- Continuing Education Activity
content: Breast mastectomy for prophylactic or curative reasons can potentially affect a patient's well-being, gender identity, and gait balance, as well as the fit and appearance of clothing. Clinicians need to recognize which patients are candidates for breast reconstruction and what options for breast reconstruction are available. This activity reviews postoperatively adjustable breast implants as one of the options for breast reconstruction. It further illustrates the important role of the interprofessional team in the management of patients who undergo breast mastectomy followed by breast reconstruction.

title: Postoperatively Adjustable Breast Implant -- Introduction
content: Breast cancer is one of the most commonly diagnosed malignancies in women around the world. In the United States, approximately 12.5% of the population is affected. [1] Therefore, genetic testing for breast cancer genes has gained popularity to identify women who are at high risk of developing breast cancer. For that reason, prophylactic mastectomies with reconstruction are being performed almost as frequently as curative mastectomies. Until 2002, the preferred method of reconstruction was performed with autologous tissue. The use of prosthetic devices, such as silicone implants, began to be utilized for breast reconstruction in the 1960s.

title: Postoperatively Adjustable Breast Implant -- Introduction
content: Implant-based reconstructions have become the more popular approach since 2008, accounting for about 65% of reconstructions. [1] [2] Implant-based reconstruction has advantages over other types of breast reconstruction in that it is a relatively easier surgery with shorter operative time; unlike autologous tissue reconstruction, there are no complications from donor sites, and the recovery is faster. This type of reconstruction preserves the skin envelope, uses a tissue expander (helping the patient select a final implant size more accurately), and allows the patient to undergo chemotherapy without delay. [3] Other factors to consider in implant-based breast reconstruction include whether it is performed as a single-stage or 2-stage approach and the implant placement, such as prepectoral vs. subpectoral.

title: Postoperatively Adjustable Breast Implant -- Anatomy and Physiology
content: The breast, or mammary gland, is located on the thorax, beneath the skin, and is considered a subcutaneous organ. Boundaries of the breast are as follows: clavicle superiorly, inframammary fold inferiorly, sternum medially, serratus anterior laterally, pectoral muscles posteriorly, and skin anteriorly. The breast spans from the second to the sixth intercostal space.

title: Postoperatively Adjustable Breast Implant -- Anatomy and Physiology
content: The subpectoral space boundary follows the pectoralis major muscle anteriorly, the rib cage and pectoralis minor posteriorly, the serratus anterior laterally, and the subcutaneous tissue inferiorly covered with the mastectomy flap. [4] The pre-pectoral space is defined as the space between the pectoralis major muscle fascia and the mastectomy flap.

title: Postoperatively Adjustable Breast Implant -- Indications
content: Bilateral breast reconstruction is better suited to the small and medium-sized breasts. If unilateral breast reconstruction is performed, the contralateral breast may necessitate mastopexy, reduction, or augmentation to achieve bilateral symmetry. Large-breasted patients can also undergo implant-based reconstruction if they are willing to undergo skin/breast reduction and contralateral surgery. [1] These patients are otherwise offered autologous tissue breast reconstruction.

title: Postoperatively Adjustable Breast Implant -- Contraindications
content: Medical conditions that can compromise the skin envelope for the breast implant include scleroderma, a history of radiation, and a history of smoking. The previously irradiated breast can lead to implant infection and extrusion; therefore, for these patients, autologous tissue reconstruction is preferred. If a patient needs adjuvant radiation therapy after mastectomy, immediate implant-based reconstruction is advised against until radiation is completed. [1] For pre-pectoral (subcutaneous) implant placement, high body mass index, history of smoking, and pre-operative radiation are absolute contraindications due to the high risk of implant extrusion. [5]

title: Postoperatively Adjustable Breast Implant -- Equipment
content: Tissue expanders are utilized to maximize skin volume before implant placement. There are two types of tissue expanders used for breast reconstruction. One is filled with compressed carbon dioxide, and the second type with saline.

title: Postoperatively Adjustable Breast Implant -- Equipment
content: Saline tissue expanders are sequentially filled with saline in the outpatient setting. This requires weekly or biweekly clinic visits to reach the desired volume. The saline infusions are performed with percutaneous needle sticks that can cause patient anxiety and discomfort as well as an increased risk of infection. Another potential complication is skin dehiscence due to the sudden expansion with saline bolus, causing pressure necrosis on mastectomy flaps. The advantages of the saline tissue expander include not requiring adjustment of the radiation therapy protocol, and the saline can be removed from the expander if indicated. [6]

title: Postoperatively Adjustable Breast Implant -- Equipment
content: Carbon dioxide expanders are remote-controlled, allowing the patient to perform gradual expansion in the outpatient or home setting. It does not require percutaneous needle sticks, thus reducing the potential for infections. The expansion is more gradual, and the volume is achieved faster than with a traditional saline tissue expander. The patients can receive adjuvant radiotherapy; however, the radiation oncologist may have to modify the radiation protocol. Another disadvantage is that carbon dioxide cannot be expelled from the tissue expander if required. [6] Unfortunately, the company filed for bankruptcy in 2019, and this product is no longer available.

title: Postoperatively Adjustable Breast Implant -- Equipment
content: Breast implant (saline vs. silicone) remains one of the more popular methods of breast reconstruction. In the case of a rupture, those with saline may feel more comfortable knowing that only saline is entering their body. Implants still tend to be a much simpler surgery comparatively. On the other hand, saline implants typically last only 10 to 15 years, are palpable, and can cause skin rippling. Silicone implants are lighter, last 20 to 25 years, and look more natural with less rippling. According to the FDA, there is a possible associated risk of developing breast-implant-associated anaplastic large cell lymphoma with either type of implant. The increased risk of developing BIA-ALCL is limited to textured implants.

title: Postoperatively Adjustable Breast Implant -- Equipment
content: The acellular dermal matrix (ADM) can be derived from porcine, bovine, or cadaveric tissue, rather than synthetic mesh. [1] ADM is indicated for soft-tissue reinforcement and allows reconstruction to remain within the breast's boundaries. ADM is an aseptic product (not sterile), which can be concerning for increased risk of infection. [7] Drains are used to remove potential fluid collections, whether they are seromas or hematomas. A variety of sizes are available, and it is the surgeon's preference on which size is utilized.

title: Postoperatively Adjustable Breast Implant -- Personnel
content: The following personnel are required for this procedure: Breast oncologic surgeon or general surgeon Plastic surgeon Operating room support team Medical/radiation oncologists

title: Postoperatively Adjustable Breast Implant -- Preparation
content: Preoperative planning requires close communication between breast oncologic surgeons, medical/radiation oncologists, and plastic surgeons. Preferably, breast margins should be marked before the patient goes under anesthesia while in the standing position. Important measurements to take into consideration are the distance from the sternal notch to the nipple, the distance between the nipple-areolar complex and the inframammary fold, and the total width of the breast. [1]

title: Postoperatively Adjustable Breast Implant -- Preparation
content: Smoking cessation is strongly advised before any type of reconstruction due to an increased risk of complications such as skin flap necrosis and infection. A window of at least three weeks between smoking cessation and breast reconstruction is recommended. [8]

title: Postoperatively Adjustable Breast Implant -- Technique or Treatment
content: After the mastectomy is completed, the skin flaps are assessed to ensure that the blood supply is not compromised. The surgeon can assess capillary refill, skin color, dermal bleeding, and skin temperature. Other techniques include laser-assisted indocyanine green or fluorescein angiography. [1]

title: Postoperatively Adjustable Breast Implant -- Technique or Treatment
content: When performing immediate breast reconstruction, there are two options: single-stage vs. 2-stage reconstruction. The 2-stage approach is most commonly performed; however, the single-stage approach is gaining popularity. [9]

The 2-stage approach is most commonly performed; however, the single-stage approach is gaining popularity. [9]

title: Postoperatively Adjustable Breast Implant -- Technique or Treatment
content: In the single-stage approach, an all-in-one adjustable tissue expander and implant are placed simultaneously. The adjustable expander has a subcutaneous port for post-operative adjustments to be performed by the patient in the outpatient setting. The benefit of this approach is that the patient undergoes only one surgical intervention under general anesthesia. The subcutaneous port can be removed in the clinic setting under local anesthesia. The complications of this approach are comparable to those of the 2-stage approach. [9]

title: Postoperatively Adjustable Breast Implant -- Technique or Treatment
content: In the 2-stage approach, the tissue expander is placed immediately after mastectomy and left in place for sequential expansion until the desired breast volume is achieved. Patients must then undergo a second surgical intervention to remove the tissue expander and replace it with permanent implants that match the breast volume achieved.

title: Postoperatively Adjustable Breast Implant -- Technique or Treatment
content: The subpectoral space (or submuscular) implant-based reconstruction is created by releasing the inferior and medial attachments of the pectoralis major muscle; the external oblique muscle aponeurosis is released inferiorly, the serratus anterior muscle laterally, and the costal cartilages medially. [4] Once this is performed, the pectoralis major can be lifted, and the pocket is dissected further cephalad, taking care not to injure the thoracoacromial bundle or the internal mammary perforators. [1]

[4] Once this is performed, the pectoralis major can be lifted, and the pocket is dissected further cephalad, taking care not to injure the thoracoacromial bundle or the internal mammary perforators. title: Postoperatively Adjustable Breast Implant -- Technique or Treatment
content: For the pre-pectoral (subcutaneous) space, the implant is attached to a mesh or acellular dermal matrix before being fixed in place. Attachment points are at the inframammary fold inferiorly and to the pectoralis major muscle fascia superiorly.

title: Postoperatively Adjustable Breast Implant -- Technique or Treatment
content: It is important to mention the use of acellular dermal matrix (ADM) or synthetic mesh in either one or 2-stage reconstruction. This is attached at the inframammary fold to create a sling for the adjustable implant/tissue expander, or it can be utilized to cover the tissue expander circumferentially. In some studies, the use of ADM/synthetic mesh has been associated with lower complication rates during subcutaneous implant placement. [5]

title: Postoperatively Adjustable Breast Implant -- Complications
content: Although the subpectoral (submuscular) placement provides an extra tissue layer over the implant and prevents the implant from migrating inferiorly, this approach also carries complications. Muscle dissection can cause an increase in postoperative pain levels. Other reported complications are animation deformity, shoulder dysfunction, and a less natural-appearing breast due to implant placement under the muscle. [5]

title: Postoperatively Adjustable Breast Implant -- Complications
content: The pre-pectoral (subcutaneous) placement allows for a more natural-appearing breast and reduces postoperative pain, as the muscle insertions are left intact. Complications associated with this approach include capsular contracture, implant loss or exposure, implant migration, and skin flap ischemia. [5]

title: Postoperatively Adjustable Breast Implant -- Complications
content: Capsular contracture is the development of an envelope of fibrous tissue around the implant, leading to breast pain and deformity. There is an increased rate of this complication in breast reconstruction versus breast augmentation patients. It has also been noted that capsular contracture occurs to a lesser degree with subpectoral placement because the muscle movement massages the implant and provides an additional layer of coverage between the implant and the skin, with the muscle acting as a barrier to bacteria. [10] The introduction of textured implants has diminished the risk of capsular contracture. The history of an irradiated breast is another predisposing factor that can lead to capsular contracture. Hematoma formation can be prevented with bulb suction drainage systems. It is important to evacuate hematomas, as they can lead to capsular contracture. [1] Complications to consider are seromas, skin flap necrosis, infection, and implant exposure/loss.

title: Postoperatively Adjustable Breast Implant -- Clinical Significance
content: With the increasing emergence of bilateral mastectomies with reconstruction, whether it is for cancer treatment or prophylactically, it is important as a general surgeon/plastic surgeon to be cognizant of different approaches to reconstruction. Breast cancer is a complex disease with very specific treatment modalities that are individualized to each patient. It is crucial to be aware of the indications and contraindications for the different types of reconstruction to determine which is most appropriate for the patient.

title: Postoperatively Adjustable Breast Implant -- Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes
content: The skills involved in post-mastectomy reconstruction with postoperative adjustable implants require specific technique and expertise, which takes time to develop. The strategy depends on the approach chosen: concomitant mastectomy reconstruction or delayed reconstruction. It is important to educate the nursing staff to monitor flap integrity postoperatively. In the preoperative preparation for any of the reconstructions, it is crucial to educate the patient on smoking cessation. Postoperatively, patient education on drain care, diabetes control, and shoulder range-of-motion exercises is important for recovery.
